name: Procyanidin B2

lead: Procyanidin B2 is a polyphenol found in apples, used in hair-growth tonics by people wanting thicker scalp hair as a natural option.

Proposed actions include protecting hair epithelial cells from TGF-beta-induced cell death and boosting keratin expression, which supports the growth phase. Research includes cell studies, apple-extract studies in mice, and a 2018 randomized trial of an Annurca apple formulation whose extracts were rich in procyanidin B2. Most of this used extracts rather than the isolated compound.

paras: It is used as a topical tonic or lotion, or as an apple extract, in a regular scalp routine. Hair changes are generally judged over months.
Procyanidins are common in food. Safety of concentrated supplements was not assessed in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Procyanidin B2 is an apple polyphenol used to stimulate the follicle growth phase for more scalp hair. Studies include cell work, mouse work and a small human trial, mostly of whole apple extracts.

lead: Procyanidin B2 is a B-type dimer of the procyanidin subgroup of proanthocyanidins, polyphenols built mainly from catechin and epicatechin units. Apples are a notable dietary source of proanthocyanidins. [1]

Apple-derived procyanidins, and procyanidin B2 in particular, have been studied for hair growth. A PubMed search listing shows research on procyanidin oligomers in hair epithelial cells, apple-extract studies in mice, and a 2018 randomized clinical trial of an Annurca apple formulation; the abstracts describe the Annurca extracts as rich in procyanidin B2. [2] Evidence is early and based largely on extracts rather than the pure compound.

paras: Procyanidins are condensed flavan-3-ols. Wikipedia lists procyanidin B2 among B-type dimers; apples contain roughly 70-141 mg proanthocyanidins per 100 g, with some of the highest levels in Red Delicious and Granny Smith varieties. [1]

A 2006 paper in Skin Pharmacology and Physiology examined procyanidin oligomers against TGF-beta-induced apoptosis in hair epithelial cells. [2] Further listed work examines Annurca apple extract effects on keratin expression in follicular cells and on hair growth in mice. [2]

A 2018 Journal of Medicinal Food paper reports a randomized clinical trial of an Annurca apple-based nutraceutical on hair growth, alongside a human skin model; it tested an extract formulation, not pure procyanidin B2. Only its title was reviewed. [2]
